question: Press publishers’ rights in Greece: Directive (EU) 2019/790 at risk of being undermined

Directive (EU) 2019/7901, which establishes a related right for press publishers to receive fair and reasonable remuneration from large online platforms using journalistic content, was transposed into Greek national law by means of Law 4996/2022.

According to recent reports, the EETT2 – as the national facilitator for setting the remuneration conditions – is considering excluding the indirect revenues of large platforms3 from the calculation of the amounts due, dramatically limiting the remuneration and rendering the related right an inadequate tool for protecting journalistic creation.

Excluding the indirect revenues of large digital platforms from the calculation for publishers’ remuneration will lead to market distortion and completely invalidate the European legislator’s intention to ensure a fair share for publishers in the digital economy. What is more, it would sabotage the goal of remedying the imbalance in bargaining power between publishers and global digital giants.
In view of this, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
Is the above-mentioned prospective change consistent with Article 154 of Directive (EU) 2019/790?
What measures does it intend to take to ensure the uniform and effective implementation of the directive and to prevent national arrangements or interpretations that undermine publishers’ rights?

Does it intend to take action, for example by issuing guidelines or clarification recommendations, to ensure that the calculation of remuneration also takes into consideration the indirect economic benefits that platforms derive from the use of journalistic content?

On copyright in the Digital Single Market. The Hellenic Telecommunications and Post Commission. E.g. revenues from advertising, promotion of content, collection of user data, etc. Setting out the need for genuinely fair compensation for press publishers.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.1.2026) Article 15 of the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market (DSM) Directive1 provides press publishers with an exclusive right to authorise or prohibit the reproduction and making available to the public of press publications in respect of online uses of such publications by information society service providers.

The objective of this rule is to facilitate the licensing and enforcement of rights in press publications when negotiating for their online use by information society service providers. Article 15 of the DSM Directive does not regulate the remuneration due for the exercise of this right.

It only provides that authors of works incorporated in press publications receive an appropriate share of the revenues received by press publishers. The Commission has been carefully monitoring the implementation of the press publishers’ right across EU Member States.

Some Member States have introduced specific rules when implementing Article 15 into their national laws, with the aim to facilitate the conclusion of licenses for the online use of press publications and ensure that press publishers are adequately remunerated.

Under Article 30(1) of the DSM Directive, the Commission is required to review the DSM Directive and present a report on its main findings no sooner than June 2026. To this effect, the Commission has recently launched a study which will support the assessment of the effectiveness and practical impact of the directive’s provisions, including Article 15.
